title: I forced Codex to blind-audit Claude’s backtests with zero memory. Here’s how it killed a +4.4%/q (t=3.0) short strategy and caught the researcher crediting transaction costs as profit
author: DiligentSloth0
selftext:
**I tested shorting SEC late filers. The backtest showed +4.37% per quarter, but the strategy failed validation—and an AI audit found a cost-sign bug.**

Across 34 historical quarters from 2016 to 2024, shorting companies that filed overdue financial reports produced a statistically significant headline return. But the strategy failed two pre-registered checks, and a separate audit raised questions about a corporate-action repair behind the result.

The research workflow used two model families. A primary researcher, running on Claude or Codex, had to specify a falsifiable market mechanism and freeze its evaluation gates before inspecting returns. After the study closed, a fresh process from the other model family audited the evidence without access to the researcher’s prior conversation history.

This is one of the studies that ended up marked **dead**.

# Round 1: The long hypothesis lost 11.9% per quarter

The original hypothesis was straightforward. When a company files a late-filing notification—SEC Form NT 10-K or NT 10-Q—risk-averse or mandate-constrained investors may sell. Once the overdue report is filed within 92 days, the delinquency is considered “cured.” The hypothesis was that accounting uncertainty would then subside and the discount would reverse.

The primary researcher tested the long trade across seven initial quarter-end windows from 2024 to 2026, covering 173 observations. Cured filers were matched against controls formed on dollar volume and prior-quarter return.

The mean quarterly net matched excess return was **−11.91%**. None of the seven windows was positive. Cured filers ranked at the 40.4th percentile of their matched cells, with a market slope of 0.03.

At least in this sample, filing the overdue report did not mark a rebound.

# Round 2: Flip the trade—and accidentally credit transaction costs

The obvious follow-up was: what if you short the same basket instead?

The preliminary short-side screen reported **+11.16% per quarter** under an adverse borrow assumption, and +13.2% per quarter in the liquid slice after excluding one outlier.

But the short direction had been chosen *after* seeing the long trade fail on the same events. That made the result an in-sample observation. A separate historical test was needed.

The independent Codex auditor later found a more basic problem in the calculation:

>“Round 2 overstates short returns. It negates Round 1’s already cost-reduced long excess, thereby crediting transaction costs. Correct subtraction reduces its adverse-borrow mean from 11.16% to 9.41% quarterly... Its timing comparison also selects formation-t survivors asymmetrically.”

The researcher had negated the already cost-reduced long return:

**Buggy short return = −(gross long return − costs) = −gross long return + costs**

That turned transaction costs into a positive contribution.

# Round 3: The historical test

The follow-up covered **June 2016 through September 2024**: 34 quarter-ends, of which 30 windows met the minimum threshold of at least 15 cured names. The sample contained **803 name-window observations**.

Before inspecting the returns, the workflow checked point-in-time CIK-to-ticker mappings against a pre-registered 97% accuracy threshold. The observed accuracy was **99.74%**, or 2,686 correct mappings out of 2,693.

Six gates were frozen before evaluation:

**S1 — Within-cell rank: PASS.** Cured filers ranked at the **45.31st percentile** of matched peers, with t = 3.43. The criterion was below the 50th percentile.

**S2 — Short spread: PASS.** The reported market-adjusted spread was **+4.37% per quarter**, with t = 3.00 and 22 of 30 windows positive, assuming 3% annual borrow.

**S3 — Market neutrality: PASS.** The control-universe slope was **−0.08**, within the maximum absolute slope of 0.25.

**S4 — Horizon fade: PASS.** Early lag was **4.60% per quarter**, versus **2.18%** later, with a Newey-West t-statistic of 3.26.

**S5 — Pre-notice placebo: FAIL.** Before filing the late notice, the same companies already ranked at the **45.43rd percentile**. The pre-registered floor was 47.65.

**S6 — Liquid tier: FAIL.** Among companies with at least **$300 million in market capitalization** and **$20 million in average daily dollar volume**, the spread was **−0.88% per quarter** across 159 observations.

The asterisks on S2 and S4 matter; more on those below.

S5 weakened the proposed event mechanism. The companies were already underperforming before the late notice, so the test did not establish that the filing created a new dislocation.

S6 challenged the economics. The liquid tier lost money, while the broad-basket result was sensitive to borrow costs. Estimated break-even borrow was roughly **20% per year**; at a 40% annual borrow assumption, the strategy lost approximately **5.1% per quarter**.

Those results do not establish the actual availability or cost of borrowing every stock in the sample, but they were enough to fail the study’s pre-registered gates.

# The Sigma Designs corporate-action bug

On the initial pass of Round 3, the mean short spread was **+1.37% per quarter**, and both S2 and S4 failed.

While inspecting an extreme outlier in the worst return window, the primary researcher found a corporate-action artifact involving **Sigma Designs (SIGM)**. In 2018, Sigma paid a cash liquidating distribution. The resulting price drop was misclassified by the researcher’s split-repair rule as an unrecorded stock split, multiplying the distribution entitlement and creating a phantom extreme return.

The researcher logged the defect and preserved the before-and-after results. The post-fix table reported **+4.37% per quarter**, and S2 and S4 changed from fail to pass. The study was still closed as dead because S5 and S6 failed.

The zero-memory Codex auditor considered the mechanical explanation credible, but challenged how the generalized repair was selected:

>“The fix followed inspection of the worst return window. Its explanation is mechanically credible: treating SIGM’s distribution-related drop as a split multiplied the dividend entitlement. Nevertheless, the generalized three-day/25% exclusion was selected after outcomes were seen, so I count it as development. Mean spread rose from 1.37% to 4.19%; S2 and S4 changed from fail to pass. Both versions are preserved, which is sound disclosure. The ‘bug’ label and continued overall failure do not establish absence of retuning; the packet cannot independently validate the chosen repair thresholds.”

The auditor also noted:

>“The fix was found by auditing only the worst outlier after results... The favorable tail was not audited, so S2’s t-statistic may be overstated.”

There is a number I still need to reconcile: the post-fix table reports **4.37% per quarter**, while the audit quote reports **4.19%**. I would want that resolved before relying on either figure.

The methodological issue remains regardless. If you investigate data errors only when they hurt the backtest, favorable errors can remain untouched. And even when the underlying artifact is real, choosing a generalized repair threshold after inspecting outcomes makes the repaired result part of the development process, rather than a clean independent confirmation.

# Verdict

**Status: Dead.**

The initial long trade lost **11.9% per quarter** in the exposed sample. The historical short test produced a headline **+4.37% per quarter**, but failed the pre-notice placebo, lost **0.88% per quarter** in the liquid tier, and depended on a post-outcome corporate-action filter to pass the spread and horizon-fade gates.

The useful finding was not that a high t-statistic is meaningless. It was that the statistic could not answer the questions the failed checks raised: whether the late filing explained the underperformance, whether the signal survived in the liquid tier, and how much confidence to place in a repair selected after inspecting the result.

Like a lot of people here, I’ve been using Claude and Codex to speed up strategy research. My biggest headache hasn't been getting them to write Python—it's how subtly they p-hack, leak future info, or negotiate with the data once they see a bad PnL.

To stop them from fooling me, I set up a local workflow where one model acts as the primary researcher (pre-registering a hypothesis and freezing pass/fail gates before touching returns), and once it finishes, a fresh, zero-memory session from the other model family is spun up as a blind auditor to tear the code and evidence apart.

Out of 138+ ideas tested this way, almost everything has died. I wanted to share one from this week (testing SEC late filers, NT 10-K / NT 10-Q) because the way it failed—and the bugs the blind auditor caught—is a textbook example of how easy it is to get fooled by an LLM backtest.

1. The initial idea that bled -11.9% a quarter

The initial hypothesis (run by Claude) was that when a company files a late-filing notice (NT 10-K/10-Q), institutions dump it, and once the overdue report is actually filed within 92 days ("cured"), the uncertainty clears and the stock rebounds.

Tested across 7 quarter-end windows (2024–2026, 173 events) against volume/prior-return matched controls, the long basket lost -11.91% per quarter net. 0 out of 7 windows were positive. They didn't rebound; they just kept bleeding.

2. Flipping it short—and the hilarious sign-flip bug

Seeing a -11.9% quarterly loss across all 7 windows, the agent naturally wanted to test the short side in Round 2. On paper, the quick screen looked amazing: +11.16% per quarter (+13.2% excluding one outlier).

When the zero-memory Codex auditor inspected the Round 2 script later, it caught a classic LLM lazy-coding bug:

>"Round 2 overstates short returns. It negates Round 1’s already cost-reduced long excess, thereby crediting transaction costs. Correct subtraction reduces its adverse-borrow mean from 11.16% to 9.41% quarterly..."

To flip the long results to short, Claude had literally just multiplied the net long return by -1:  
short\_return = -(gross\_long - costs) = -gross\_long + costs

By negating the net series, it turned transaction costs into a positive profit rebate.

3. The 34-quarter out-of-sample replication (2016–2024)

Because flipping from long to short after seeing Round 1 fail is textbook in-sample snooping, the workflow forced an out-of-sample replication on unseen 2016–2024 data (34 quarters, 803 observations) with 6 pre-registered gates (S1–S6) that all had to pass:

|Gate|Requirement|Result|Pass?|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|S1: Cell Rank|Lag matched peers (< 50th pct)|45.31st pct (t = 3.43)|Yes|
|S2: Short Spread|\> 0% net at 3%/yr borrow|\+4.37%/q (t = 3.00, 22/30 pos)|Yes|
|S3: Market Beta|Control slope within ±0.25|\-0.08|Yes|
|S4: Horizon Fade|Q+1/Q+2 lag > Q+3/Q+4 lag|4.60% vs 2.18% (NW t = 3.26)|Yes|
|S5: Pre-Notice Check|No lag before the NT notice (≥ 47.65)|45.43rd pct|NO|
|S6: Liquid Borrowable|Profitable in Cap ≥ $300M, ADV ≥ $20M|\-0.88%/q (159 obs)|NO|

If you only looked at S1–S4, you’d think you found a holy grail: +4.37% a quarter over 8.5 years out-of-sample with a t-stat of 3.00 and zero market beta.

But S5 and S6 killed it:

* S5 (Selection bias): These stocks were already at the 45.43rd percentile in the quarter before filing the late notice. The notice wasn't a catalyst; these were just chronically dying companies.
* S6 (The borrow cliff): Almost all the +4.37%/q gain sat in illiquid micro-caps where borrow is either unavailable or 20–40%/yr. In liquid, easy-to-borrow names (≥300Mcap,≥300Mcap,≥ 20M daily volume), the return was -0.88% a quarter.

1. The Sigma Designs (+2,455%) liquidation bug & asymmetric bug-hunting

Notice the asterisks on S2 and S4. On the first pass of Round 3, the mean short spread was only +1.37%/q and S2/S4 failed.

While checking the worst outlier window, Claude found that in 2018, Sigma Designs (SIGM) paid a cash liquidating distribution. Because the stock dropped >90% ex-distribution, the split-repair rule misread the liquidation payout as an unrecorded stock split, creating a fake +2,455% outlier. Claude logged the fix (keeping both pre-fix and post-fix tables per protocol), which bumped the spread from +1.37% to +4.37%.

When the blind Codex auditor reviewed this patch, it refused to let it slide as a clean bug fix:

>"The fix followed inspection of the worst return window. Its explanation is mechanically credible: treating SIGM’s distribution-related drop as a split multiplied the dividend entitlement. Nevertheless, the generalized three-day/25% exclusion was selected after outcomes were seen, so I count it as development... Furthermore, the fix was found by auditing only the worst outlier after results. The favorable tail was not audited, so S2’s t-statistic may be overstated."

That last line hit hard: if you only hunt for data bugs when an outlier hurts your backtest, and never audit the outliers that make you money, you're biasing your t-stat upward even when the bug itself is 100% real.

Anyway, this idea is officially dead and buried in the graveyard with the other 137 studies. I put the static viewer and the raw cross-audit logs up on GitHub ([https://github.com/quoituparle/DeadGuess](https://github.com/quoituparle/DeadGuess)) and [visualized reports](https://deadguess.com/) if anyone wants to poke through the full reports.

Curious how others here handle corporate-action edge cases like liquidating distributions in historical equities data, or if anyone else is using adversarial LLM setups to audit their own research code?
